// Roll a subgenre first, then everything else inside it. The old brief rolled a
// flat "wrongness" seed and a quiet ending, which locked every story into one
// subgenre (institutional dread, nothing ever seen). Now each subgenre carries its
// own threat seeds and ending types so the combination coheres, and the feed
// alternates realistic horror with supernatural horror.
//
// mode picks which worked example the prompt shows:
//   realistic-dread     present tense, nothing impossible is ever confirmed
//   supernatural-reveal present tense, the thing is seen or named before the end
//   confession-past     past tense, told afterwards, ends on one line that recasts it

  {

    cores: [
      "a door that was locked is now unlocked from the inside",
      "the narrator finds a sleeping bag under their own bed",
      "food is missing from the fridge every morning, a little at a time",
      "the baby monitor picks up breathing from an empty room",
      "the narrator's spare key is in the lock from the outside",
      "there are footprints in the dust of the attic, going in, none coming out",
      "the dog stares at the crawlspace hatch and will not eat",
      "the narrator's phone shows a Wi-Fi device called BEDROOM that they never set up",
      "someone has been sleeping in the narrator's bed while they are at work - the sheets are warm",
      "the smoke alarm chirps only at 3 a.m., and the battery is always new"

    endings: [
      "cut-off: the narrator hears the sound again and the story stops mid-action",
      "hard reveal: the narrator finally sees the person and the person is already looking at them",
      "twist: the intruder has been there longer than the narrator has lived in the house",
      "quiet implication: the narrator locks the door, knowing it will not matter"

const EXAMPLES = {

    brief: `SUBGENRE: institutional uncanny - systems and care that cannot be refused
WHAT MAY APPEAR: nothing impossible is ever confirmed
THE THREAT: a food delivery arrives that was never ordered
SETTING: a ground-floor apartment
TENSE: present
HOW IT ENDS: quiet implication - the narrator does what the note instructed`,
    text: `The delivery app says my order was completed at 2:14 a.m. I did not order anything, and I was asleep at 2:14. I check the door anyway. There is a paper bag on the mat, still warm, my name on the receipt above the line CUSTOMER PREFERS NO CONTACT. I bring it inside and set it on the counter. Inside is a container of soup, a plastic spoon, and a napkin folded into quarters. I unfold the napkin. It is a list, handwritten, of everything I have eaten this week. Tuesday's noodles. The two coffees on Thursday. The apple I did not finish. At the bottom, under today's date, someone has written soup, and drawn a small empty box beside it. I stand at the counter holding the napkin. Then I take the lid off the container and pick up the spoon.`
  },
  "supernatural-reveal": {
    brief: `SUBGENRE: doppelganger / mimic - something is copying a person
WHAT MAY APPEAR: the mimic may be seen; it gets small details wrong
THE THREAT: the narrator's neighbour's skin is being worn by something too tall for it
SETTING: family home - owned
TENSE: present
HOW IT ENDS: quiet implication - the narrator goes back inside`,
    text: `My neighbour has been standing at my back fence since noon. It is nine at night now. I watched him through the kitchen window while I made lunch, then dinner, and he did not move. Not to scratch. Not to shift his weight. His porch light came on at eight, on its timer. I go out because the dog needs to go out. The dog stops on the top step and will not come down. I say his name. Dave. He turns his head toward me, then his shoulders, then his hips, one after the other, like something working out how a body is put together. His face is Dave's face. It is too smooth around the mouth and it sits a little too far down his neck. He smiles, and the smile keeps going past where a mouth should stop. He rests one arm on top of the fence. The fence is six feet high. I go back inside and I do not turn on the lights.`
  },
  "confession-past": {
    brief: `SUBGENRE: true crime - the man next door, told afterwards
WHAT MAY APPEAR: a real criminal; violence implied, never shown
THE THREAT: a repairman who asked which bedroom was the child's
SETTING: family home - owned
TENSE: past
HOW IT ENDS: aftermath line - one sentence that recasts everything`,
    text: `The man who fixed our furnace in 1998 asked my mother for a glass of water, then asked to use the bathroom, then asked how many bedrooms we had. I was nine. I remember because he crouched down to my height and asked which one was mine. My mother said third door on the left, laughing, the way you do. He said he would remember that. He was in the house forty minutes. That night the furnace worked fine. It worked fine for eleven years. When we sold the house, the inspector found a crawlspace under the utility room that was not on any plan, about the size of a single mattress, with a vent cut into the floor of the third bedroom on the left. There was a sleeping bag. There was a shoebox of photographs, all of a girl asleep, all taken from below. The police dated them from 1998 to 2009. I moved out in 2009.`
  }
};

const pick = a => a[Math.floor(Math.random() * a.length)];

// 50/50 between families so the feed alternates, then uniform inside the family.
const family = Math.random() < 0.5 ? "realistic" : "supernatural";
const genre  = pick(GENRES.filter(g => g.family === family));

// Measured at 3.72 words/second across stories 4-36 (edge-tts, RATE=+40%).
// 170 words is about 46 seconds of narration.
const TARGET_WORDS = 170;

// Asking for a single number lands within a few percent. Asking for a RANGE
// ("150-170 words") made it undershoot to ~86%. Keep the exact number.
const ASK_WORDS = Math.round(TARGET_WORDS * 1.0);

return [{ json: { decisions: {
  genre:        genre.id,
  family:       genre.family,
  mode:         genre.mode,
  tense:        genre.tense,
  pitch:        genre.pitch,
  allow:        genre.allow,
  core:         pick(genre.cores),
  ending:       pick(genre.endings),
  setting:      pick(settings),
  example_brief: EXAMPLES[genre.mode].brief,
  example_text:  EXAMPLES[genre.mode].text,
  target_words: TARGET_WORDS,
  ask_words:    ASK_WORDS
} } }];

values.content: You write horror monologues for narrated short-form video, under one minute each. First person, one narrator, spoken aloud. The first sentence must stop a scroll: a specific, concrete, disturbing fact. Concrete detail over adjectives. Never explain the scare. Never tell the listener what to feel.

parameters.content:
## Genre first, then everything else

The Randomizer rolls a family (realistic / supernatural, 50/50), then one of
18 subgenres inside it. Each subgenre carries its own threat seeds, ending
types, tense and a worked example (mode), so the brief coheres: a creature
story shows the creature; an institutional story never confirms anything.

One call, one example. Five-pass chains drifted on a 14B model, and
qwen2.5-14b ignores negative rules ("don't say realized") but matches an
example. The example is inlined in the user message: the Responses API node
wraps every message as input_text, so an assistant turn 400s.

Violence stays implied - explicit gore gets shorts demonetised or removed.

decisions.genre / family are passed through Clean and Measure as brief.*
for captions and hashtags later.

## Length

170 words is about 46 seconds at RATE=+40%
(3.72 words/sec, measured across stories 4-36).

Change TARGET_WORDS in the Randomizer to retarget:
  110 words = 30s
  170 words = 46s
  220 words = 60s
